Redux Concepts in

If you are familiar with Redux, most of your architectural knowledge transfers directly to . The primary difference is not conceptual — it is structural.

This page is designed to help you bridge your understanding between Redux and . It is not a step-by-step migration guide. Instead, it explains how common Redux concepts map to constructs so you can reason about both systems clearly.

Redux centralizes state through a global store and reducer tree. scopes state to independent FeatureCells and executes updates through a deterministic pipeline.

Reducers, pure functions, selectors, and immutable state principles all remain valid. In many cases, existing reducer logic and transformation functions can be reused without modification, provided they remain pure and deterministic.

Redux and can run side by side within the same application. You are not required to migrate existing stores immediately. New state can be implemented using FeatureCells while existing Redux stores continue operating unchanged. Over time, you may choose to convert specific slices — or run both systems in parallel to validate behavior before switching fully.

It may initially feel unusual not to write action creators, switch statements, or boilerplate-heavy reducer composition. That difference is intentional. reduces ceremony by formalizing execution inside the pipeline rather than requiring repetitive structural code. The reduced surface area is not a simplification of capability — it is a simplification of mechanics.

Plain TypeScript. Zero Magic. That is the design constraint. does not rely on hidden runtime behavior, implicit mutation, or framework-level interception. What you write is what executes. Pure functions stay pure. Side effects are explicit. Execution is observable. The goal is not abstraction for its own sake — it is clarity.

Diagrams
↑ top
State
↑ top

Redux

State is stored in a single global Store. Reducers combine into a root reducer, producing a single immutable tree.

State is owned by independent FeatureCells. Each FeatureCell maintains its own isolated state and execution lifecycle.

Instead of combining reducers into a single tree, you define multiple FeatureCells. Each cell is independently initialized and executed.

Your state shapes remain the same. The structural difference is where ownership lives.

Actions
↑ top

Redux

Actions are plain objects describing state transitions. They are dispatched globally and interpreted by reducers within the root store. 

{{`{ type: 'ADD_USER', payload: user }`}}

Because Redux uses a single global store, every action is broadcast to the entire reducer tree. Each reducer decides whether to respond based on the action type.

does not use global action objects. Instead, state updates are invoked directly on a specific FeatureCell using mergeState() or replaceState(). 

{{`vault.replaceState(nextValue)

or

vault.mergeState(partialValue)`}}

Each FeatureCell owns its own state. When you invoke mergeState(), you are explicitly updating that FeatureCell — not broadcasting an event to a global store.

This removes ambiguity. The update target is always clear because the method is called on the state owner itself.

If you prefer action-like structures for organization or traceability, you may still structure your input objects that way. However, they are passed directly into the owning FeatureCell rather than dispatched globally.

That said, is intentionally designed to minimize structural boilerplate. Action creators, switch statements, and large type unions are not required for correctness. It is generally recommended to avoid recreating Redux-style ceremony unless it provides clear value for your application.

Dispatch
↑ top

Redux

dispatch(action) sends an action through middleware and the reducer tree. Because Redux uses a single global store, every dispatched action is broadcast to all reducers. 

{{`dispatch({ type: 'ADD_USER', payload: user })`}}

Each reducer decides whether to respond based on the action type. Execution order may be influenced by middleware composition and reducer structure.

does not use global dispatch. Instead, state updates are invoked directly on the owning FeatureCell.

Updates are triggered by calling:

  • mergeState()
  • replaceState()
{{`vault.replaceState(nextValue)

or

vault.mergeState(partialValue)`}}

When you call mergeState(), you are explicitly updating that specific FeatureCell — not broadcasting an event to a global store.

This makes the update target unambiguous. The state owner is known at the call site, and execution flows through a deterministic pipeline rather than a reducer tree.

Instead of dispatching an action object, you submit state input into the pipeline. The conductor serializes execution, and the pipeline finalizes each attempt in a controlled microtask boundary.

Boilerplate-heavy dispatch patterns are not required for correctness. favors direct, explicit state invocation over ceremony-based event broadcasting.

Reducers
↑ top

Redux

Reducers in Redux are pure functions that compute the next state from the current state and an action.

Reducers are typically composed into a root reducer tree and executed whenever dispatch() is called.

Advanced Redux setups may dynamically inject reducers at runtime, replace reducer trees, or alter store structure during application execution.

In , reducers exist as a dedicated Reducer Stage within the pipeline.

Reducer functions remain pure and deterministic. Existing Redux reducer logic can typically be reused without modification as long as:

  • They are pure
  • They do not mutate state
  • They preserve structural shape

However, reducers in are registered declaratively through the fluent .reducers() API and must be configured before the FeatureCell is initialized. 

{{`featureCell
  .reducers([
    (current) => ({ ...current, count: current.count + 1 })
  ])
  .initialize()`}}

Reducers are not dynamically injected into the pipeline. Once initialize() is called, the pipeline structure is fixed.

This guarantees that reducer execution order is stable and deterministic for the lifetime of the FeatureCell.

Unlike Redux reducer trees, which may be composed or replaced at runtime, enforces pipeline consistency. Reducers cannot be added, removed, or reordered after initialization.

This constraint ensures:

  • Predictable execution ordering
  • Stable state derivation rules
  • No hidden runtime mutations of state logic
  • Deterministic pipeline guarantees

Reducers are the only stage permitted to produce the committed state value They never control scheduling, never emit snapshots directly, and never influence pipeline flow.

Effects
↑ top

Redux

Effects are implemented through middleware (Thunk, Saga, Observable). They handle asynchronous operations and dispatch new actions.

Asynchronous input is handled through Resolve behaviors, Interceptors, or Controllers.

Instead of middleware dispatching new actions at arbitrary times, asynchronous results enter the pipeline as controlled attempts.

Side effects remain possible, but execution is serialized and finalized consistently.

Execution Model

Unlike Redux middleware or effects libraries, asynchronous resolution in is coordinated by the pipeline itself.

Async inputs are resolved under pipeline coordination before state commitment occurs. State commitment is deferred to a microtask boundary, ensuring that observers never see partial results and that reentrancy is structurally impossible.

For a detailed explanation of these guarantees, see:

  • Pipeline Execution Guarantee

Selectors
↑ top

Redux

Selectors derive computed state from the global store. They are often memoized using libraries such as Reselect to avoid unnecessary recomputation.

Because Redux uses a single store, selectors typically receive the entire state tree and project a subset of it.

In , state is owned by individual FeatureCells, not a global store. Derived state is therefore scoped to the FeatureCell that owns it.

A FeatureCell can be injected wherever it is needed, and its state APIs are reactive across the entire application.

  • .state — synchronous immutable snapshot
  • .state$ — reactive observable stream
  • .state.value() — Angular signal (when using /angular)

Because the FeatureCell itself is injectable, any component, service, or controller that injects it receives the same reactive state source.

Derived state can be implemented using:

  • Plain TypeScript functions
  • Computed signals (Angular)
  • RxJS operators on .state$
  • Getter methods colocated with the FeatureCell

Memoization strategies remain valid. However, because state updates are atomic and deterministic, recomputation behavior is easier to reason about.

Selectors are not global projections — they are scoped, reusable views of a specific state owner.

This eliminates the need for a global selector registry and avoids tight coupling to a centralized store structure.

Store Setup
↑ top

Redux

A global Store is created using createStore() and reducer composition.

There is no monolithic root store.

Instead:

  • Initialize Vault once.
  • Register FeatureCells individually.

FeatureCells can run alongside Redux during gradual adoption.

{{`// app.config.ts

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService,
      {
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: [] 
      }
    )
  ]
};`}}
 
{{`Vault({
  devMode: true,
  logLevel: 'debug'
});

export const employeeCell = FeatureCell({
  key: 'employees',
  initialState: [],
});`}}

Components
↑ top

Redux

Components subscribe to the global Store using hooks (useSelector, useDispatch) or higher-order components (connect).

State selection and dispatch logic are typically colocated in the component or abstracted into selector files. Every dispatched action is broadcast to the entire reducer tree, and subscribed components re-evaluate selectors on each store update.

A Provider must wrap the application to supply the Store instance.

Components do not connect to a global store. Instead, they inject or import the specific FeatureCell whose state they depend on.

Because FeatureCells are state owners, a component interacts directly with the state it cares about — not a centralized root tree.

State can be consumed through:

  • cell.state — synchronous immutable snapshot
  • cell.state$ — reactive observable stream
  • cell.state.value() — Angular signal (if applicable)

There is no global store Provider requirement and no store-wide broadcast. Updates are scoped to the owning FeatureCell.

Because state commitment is atomic and deferred to a microtask, components never observe intermediate values or partially reduced state. Every render sees a finalized snapshot.

The mental model shifts from:

  • Subscribe to a global store and select a slice

to:

  • Inject the state owner and consume it directly

This reduces wiring, eliminates dispatch plumbing, and keeps state access explicit and localized.

Testing
↑ top

Redux

Reducers are tested as pure functions. Async logic is typically tested through mocked middleware (thunks, sagas, observables) or by asserting dispatch sequences.

Complex flows often require mock stores, fake timers, middleware orchestration, and manual resolution of async behavior.

Reducers remain pure and directly testable. Existing reducer tests can typically be reused without modification.

Asynchronous resolution does not require middleware mocking. All state input flows through a deterministic pipeline.

Pipeline execution can be explicitly awaited using:

  • vaultSettled()
  • flushVaultPipeline()

Because execution is serialized and state commitment is atomic, tests do not need to account for reentrancy, partial state visibility, or interleaved async commits.

Each pipeline attempt either commits a complete snapshot or produces no visible state change. This makes outcome-based testing straightforward.

Instead of asserting dispatched action sequences, tests can assert final state directly.
